episode_title: Inside the Hearts of Men and Women

stories.topic: The pro-divorce column and the hunt for odd empowerment metrics
stories.summary: Years ago Amit wrote a controversial column arguing that India's rising divorce rates were a good thing. That idea grew into a Seen and the Unseen episode, 'Metrics of Empowerment', where he and three friends looked for unusual data points that show how much agency women have. The ideas included solo travel by women, which Amit notes is rising. Nidhi Gupta suggested counting how many families have a male last child. Hamsini Hariharan suggested counting women in prisons. Another idea was how many men download BigBasket, which Amit then questions: in traditional homes the man may download the app only because he pays, then hands the phone to his wife to pick the groceries.
stories.insight: A number that sounds bad, like divorces or women in jail, can be a sign of freedom. A number that sounds good, like men ordering groceries, can hide the same old patriarchy. What matters is who is actually choosing.
stories.quote: Because to me, rising divorce rates are a sign of women's empowerment. It means more and more women are getting the agency and empowerment to leave bad marriages and it's fantastic.

stories.topic: Who really decided to order the pizza?
stories.summary: Responding to Amit's BigBasket caveat, Ajay recalls an example from their Life Lessons course. Ordering pizza involves a chain of decisions: someone decides 'let's have pizza', someone decides 'let's order Domino's', and someone places the order on the app. If the men make the first two decisions and tell the woman to place the order, her using the app shows nothing about her agency.
stories.insight: A digital record shows who tapped the button, not who made the decision. To measure agency you have to separate out each step of the decision.
stories.quote: So there is a decision that let's have pizza. There is the decision that let's order Domino's.

stories.topic: Office air conditioning was set for men in suits
stories.summary: Amit proposes a new metric: the default temperature of office air conditioning. When AC became common in offices in the 1950s and 60s, settings were designed for men in suits, and men prefer it colder because of different metabolic rates. This is the source of the familiar marital argument where the wife says she's cold and the husband says put on a sweater. He would like defaults to drift upward until both sexes are comfortable, though he admits he doesn't know how to measure this at scale.
stories.insight: Everyday infrastructure quietly builds in assumptions about who it serves. Watching those defaults change is a way to track social change.
stories.quote: when air conditioning became common in offices in the nineteen fifties and sixties, it was designed for men in suits.

stories.topic: A camera on the pavement to count women in public
stories.summary: Ajay describes a measurement idea he hasn't built yet but thinks is feasible. Point a telephoto camera at a stretch of pavement and use image classification to count passers-by and classify their gender. That gives two things: the share of people in public who are women, and how that share falls as evening comes in. He connects it to his work on crime victimisation surveys, which ask parents what time their teenage daughter should be home. That answer reflects both social norms and how safe parents think the streets are.
stories.insight: How many women are out in public, especially after dark, is a simple, continuous measure of how free a society is. With today's tools it is a small piece of software waiting to be written.
stories.quote: And then there could be these cameras all over the world just quietly purring and producing daily data for the presence of women in the public square.

stories.summary: Amit retells findings from Seth Stephens-Davidowitz. Four years before Trump's 2016 rise, Google showed many people searching for a racial slur alongside Obama's victory rather than 'first black president', concentrated in states that later voted a particular way. After the most recent US election, Stephens-Davidowitz wrote in The Economist that searches beat the polls. In states where people searched 'Trump Harris debate', Trump won. Where they searched 'Harris Trump debate', Harris won.
stories.insight: Small details of anonymous behaviour, even the order of words in a search, can reveal what surveys miss. It is the kind of signal humans would never think to look for but machines can find.
stories.quote: For example, he showed that in the states where people searched for the Trump Harris debate, Trump won. In the states where they searched for the Harris Trump debate, Harris won.

stories.topic: Comparing Google autocomplete in India and Australia
stories.summary: Amit tried the book's experiment himself, using Google autocomplete in an incognito window and switching his VPN between countries. When the book was written, India's top completion for 'my husband wants' was a request to be breastfed. Today it is 'serve his mistress', with breastfeeding at number two. The book reports that porn searches for women breastfeeding men are four times higher in India and Bangladesh than anywhere else, which Amit says he cannot explain. With the VPN set to Australia, the results included 'an open marriage', 'a second wife', 'an open marriage novel' and something far stranger. Ajay asks whether VPNs could compare Indian states, and Amit thinks that could be a research project.
stories.insight: Basic urges are shared, but culture shapes how they show up. Anyone can examine a country's private preoccupations from home for free.
stories.quote: porn searches for depictions of women breastfeeding men are four times higher in India and Bangladesh than in any other country in the world.

stories.topic: Why parents were furious about his anti-children column
stories.summary: Amit once wrote a column, partly to provoke, arguing that it is immoral to have children, and many parents were angry. Everybody Lies helped him understand why. People are seven times more likely to ask Google whether they will regret not having children than whether they will regret having them. Yet adults with children are 3.6 times more likely to tell Google they regret their choice than adults without children.
stories.insight: Strong backlash can be a sign that an argument touched a private regret. What people say about parenthood in public and what they type alone can be very different.
stories.quote: Adults with children are three point six times more likely to tell Google they regret their decision than are adults without children.

stories.topic: From lonely misfit to friends found online
stories.summary: Amit describes growing up limited to communities of circumstance: you are born somewhere, go to the local school and work where you work. As someone whose interests nobody around him shared, he was a loner until early adulthood. The internet let him form communities of choice. Most of his friends today are people he met online, and he and Ajay, though both in Bombay, met through the internet (not, he adds, on a dating app).
stories.insight: For people who don't fit in locally, the internet's biggest gift was escaping the limits of geography. Dating apps apply the same shift to romance.
stories.quote: If I'm a weirdo of some sort or if I have interests that no one else shares, I'm basically a loner as I was till my early adulthood, in fact

stories.topic: The student who wouldn't date anyone from her college
stories.summary: Amit recalls a quote from a dating survey. A young woman explained that she used dating apps instead of dating classmates because if it didn't work out she would see the man every day, possibly with another girl. An app lets her date someone she will never run into again.
stories.insight: Part of what dating apps offer is an easy exit. Being able to leave without social cost makes people more willing to try, especially women who would otherwise be judged within a small circle.
stories.quote: Look, I have to go on a dating app because I don't want to date someone from my college because if it doesn't work out, I will have to see him every day, and I might even have to see him with another girl every day.

stories.topic: A friend's real answer about age preferences
stories.summary: Dating studies say women look for men about their own age, while men of every age look for women in their early twenties (OkCupid found 21). Amit found this doubtful and asked a friend. She said women want to be seen with same-age men because it is socially acceptable, since a date at Starbucks with someone much older or younger looks odd. Personally, though, she prefers men who are either much older or much younger.
stories.insight: Even app data can reflect appearances. What people choose in public may be the socially safe choice rather than what they actually want.
stories.quote: she said that in her personal case she prefers to be with men who are either much older or much younger.

stories.topic: Amit's early trip into the manosphere
stories.summary: About twenty-five years ago, Amit got absorbed in what is now called the manosphere. He read Neil Strauss's The Game, a bestselling handbook for pickup artists that he calls basically a manual for manipulating women, but one that also showed a real understanding of human nature. That world has since grown into a large social-media industry, with advice books sold on places like Gumroad. Amit says the show Adolescence captured only a small part of it.
stories.insight: The manosphere grows out of real resentment among men who get little attention on dating apps. For many of them dating has become a game to win by any means rather than a search for love.
stories.quote: It's no longer about how to find love because they've just given up.

stories.topic: Months in Delhi, weeks in Mumbai, days in Bangalore
stories.summary: In Unboxing Bengaluru, Malini Goyal studied Tinder data from three cities, measuring how long people took to go to each other's homes after matching. It took months in Delhi, weeks in Mumbai and days in Bangalore. Amit lists possible reasons: Delhi is a low-trust society, housing in Mumbai is at a premium, and many singles in Bangalore live alone. When she then interviewed users, she found extreme promiscuity but nobody happy. People became jaded and stopped working through conflicts, because ten other matches were always chatting in real time.
stories.insight: Too much choice can undermine relationships. Building one means working through friction, and an app full of alternatives makes giving up easier than staying.
stories.quote: In Delhi it was a matter of months. In Mumbai it was a matter of weeks. In Bangalore it was a matter of days.

recommendations.item: Everybody Lies
recommendations.creator: Seth Stephens-Davidowitz
recommendations.context: The main source for the chapter on what anonymous search data reveals.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it phenomenal because of its central idea: people are most honest when searching anonymously, so search data reveals human nature in a way surveys can't. Its findings range from sexless marriages to parents' gender bias.

recommendations.item: The Truth About Ourselves
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His essay on Everybody Lies, written for Pragati when he edited it, linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: Many of the findings Amit reads out in the episode are quoted from this essay.

recommendations.item: Polls get elections wrong. So use Google
recommendations.creator: Seth Stephens-Davidowitz
recommendations.context: Stephens-Davidowitz's Economist column after the recent US election.
recommendations.reason: It shows search data beating polls: the word order 'Trump Harris debate' versus 'Harris Trump debate' tracked which candidate won each state.

recommendations.item: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His old controversial column that opens the episode.
recommendations.reason: It argues that rising divorce means more women can leave bad marriages, the starting point for looking at empowerment through unusual metrics.

recommendations.item: It is immoral to have children. Here's why
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His deliberately provocative column, revisited alongside the data on parental regret.
recommendations.reason: He says the search data on regret finally explained why parents were so angry about it.

recommendations.context: His episode with three friends on unusual data points about women's empowerment.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ashwini Deshpande
recommendations.context: Linked alongside the other workforce episodes.
recommendations.reason: An economist's view of the puzzle of women's labour-force participation in India.

recommendations.item: Crime Victimisation in India
recommendations.creator: Edited by Ajay Shah et al
recommendations.context: Ajay mentions his edited book while explaining crime victimisation surveys.
recommendations.reason: Source of the survey question about what time parents think their teenage daughter should be home, which he treats as a measure of women's empowerment.

recommendations.item: Google Trends
recommendations.creator: Google
recommendations.context: Ajay follows up on Amit's advice to run search experiments yourself.
recommendations.reason: You can save a search as a fixed URL and rerun it to see what the world is paying attention to over time.

recommendations.item: Google Autocomplete experiments (incognito window, optionally with a VPN)
recommendations.creator: Google
recommendations.context: Amit urges listeners to try the Everybody Lies experiment themselves.
recommendations.reason: In an incognito window autocomplete isn't biased by your history, and a VPN shows other countries' results. You don't need special access to Google's data to learn something.

recommendations.item: Adolescence
recommendations.creator: Jack Thorne & Stephen Graham
recommendations.context: Brought up while discussing incels and the manosphere.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it an awesome show that depicts a small part of the manosphere, which grows out of real resentment on dating apps.

recommendations.item: The Game
recommendations.creator: Neil Strauss
recommendations.context: Recalled from his time exploring the manosphere 25 years ago.
recommendations.reason: It is a manipulative pickup-artist handbook but shows a real understanding of human nature, and helps explain where today's manosphere came from.

recommendations.item: Rob Henderson's tweet on dark triad men and dating apps
recommendations.creator: Rob Henderson
recommendations.context: Amit reads it out in full in the dating-apps chapter.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it fantastic. It explains how a minority of manipulative men can push everyone on dating apps toward mutual mistreatment.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned when introducing Rob Henderson, who coined the term 'luxury beliefs'.
recommendations.reason: Background on a thinker Amit says has thought deeply about this subject.

recommendations.item: The Romantic Recession report
recommendations.context: A 2024 survey cited in the dating-apps chapter.
recommendations.reason: It documents falling trust among singles: women avoiding dating strangers, and men feeling women don't give them a fair chance.

recommendations.item: Studies on dating trends (Pew 2023, SoulMatcher 2025, OkCupid 2017, GDI 2025, Tinder 2025, IJCHP 2024)
recommendations.context: Amit says he will link the studies behind his dating-app findings.
recommendations.reason: Sources for the findings on age preferences, swipe rates and the Tinder Gini coefficient.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned while discussing marriage as a bundle that is coming apart.
recommendations.reason: Where they earlier discussed how society might organise relationships once love, sex, companionship and parenting are separated.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Malini Goyal
recommendations.context: Malini Goyal is introduced as a former guest before her Tinder research.
recommendations.reason: Background on the author of the Tinder study of three cities.

recommendations.item: Unboxing Bengaluru
recommendations.creator: Malini Goyal & Prashanth Prakash
recommendations.context: Amit calls it an excellent book.
recommendations.reason: Its Tinder data and interviews show how dating differs across Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore, and that the promiscuity on apps came with unhappiness.

recommendations.item: Finding Love in Modern India — Ep 401 of The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Sanjana Ramachandran
recommendations.context: Amit calls it an excellent episode.
recommendations.reason: A detailed look at how hard dating apps are, and how they are hard in different ways for men and women.

recommendations.item: Famous Last Questions
recommendations.creator: Sanjana Ramachandran
recommendations.context: Amit notes his guest has since written a book on finding love in modern India.
recommendations.reason: A longer treatment of modern Indian dating.

recommendations.item: When Harry Met Sally
recommendations.creator: Rob Reiner
recommendations.context: Introduces the chapter on whether men and women can be friends.
recommendations.reason: Amit loves it and calls it a charming film. Its premise that men and women can't be friends gave the Facebook friendship index its nickname.

recommendations.item: The Facebook study on Cross-Gender Social Ties
recommendations.context: A cross-gender friendship index built from 1.8 billion users and 1.4 trillion connections.
recommendations.reason: Ajay is excited because the data goes down to the smallest administrative units. He thinks researchers should use it as a standard measure of how separated men and women are in Indian cities and districts.

recommendations.item: Can men and women be just friends?
recommendations.creator: The Economist
recommendations.context: Amit calls it a beautiful piece.
recommendations.reason: It explains the Facebook index and proposes naming it after When Harry Met Sally.

recommendations.item: Parade's End
recommendations.creator: Ford Madox Ford
recommendations.context: Ajay reads a passage from it about whether men and women can talk without becoming lovers.
recommendations.reason: The passage argues that real intimate conversation needs years of living together. Amit's response: 'Beautiful. You have a romantic soul in you.'

recommendations.item: Gurwinder Bhogal quoting Christ Williamson on hiding your true self
recommendations.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes for Amit's point that you can't be loved if you hide who you are. On air he thinks Paul Graham may have said it.
recommendations.reason: It links search data, where people's hidden selves show up, to a point about why being authentic matters for being loved.

recommendations.item: Novels of Georges Simenon
recommendations.creator: Georges Simenon
recommendations.context: In his closing argument Amit calls Simenon one of his favourite novelists of all time.
recommendations.reason: Amit says Simenon's work keeps returning to the idea that no person can fully communicate himself to another, which he sees as one of humanity's great problems.

recommendations.item: The Nighttime Lights of Russia — Ep 116 of Everything is Everything
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay opens by recalling their episode on nighttime lights data.
recommendations.reason: Part of their series on measurement. Later in the episode he contrasts satellite measurement, which doesn't affect what it observes, with dating apps, which do.

recommendations.item: What Our Genes and Phones Tell Us — Ep 117 of Everything is Everything
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The previous episode, about the 'digital exhaust' of modern life.
recommendations.reason: This episode was split off from it because they had too much material for one show.

recommendations.item: Life Lessons
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's pizza example of agency comes from a discussion in the course.
recommendations.reason: The course is where they work through ideas like how to separate out who actually makes a decision.

core_ideas.explanation: Good empowerment metrics ask who is choosing. Some numbers that sound bad signal freedom: rising divorce, more women in prison, more women travelling alone. Some that sound good can hide patriarchy: men downloading grocery apps or women placing pizza orders that men decided on. Office AC temperatures and the share of women on the street at night are other indirect measures.
core_ideas.quote: More women in prisons is a good thing because it means more women have agency, more women have opportunity to commit crime and to go out in the world

core_ideas.concept: Richer families pull women out of work
core_ideas.explanation: Women's labour-force participation in India rose and then fell sharply, even as incomes grew. Amit stresses there are many causes. One is that once a family can afford it, a working wife is seen as hurting the family's honour, so women's earnings help raise the family's status and that status then keeps them at home.
core_ideas.quote: many families when they reached a certain income level, it was felt that now the woman doesn't need to go out and work. That it affects the family honour if the woman is going out and working.

core_ideas.concept: Search data reveals the secret self
core_ideas.explanation: Amit cites Gabriel García Márquez's idea that we have a public self, a private self known to a few intimates, and a secret self known to nobody. Stephens-Davidowitz's premise is that anonymous searching is where the secret self shows, because nobody is watching. On Facebook people present their best lives. Search data shows sexless marriages, regret and anxiety.
core_ideas.quote: Gabriel Garcia Marquez often talks about how we have three selves, a public self, the private self, and the secret self, right?

core_ideas.concept: What searches reveal about sex and intimacy
core_ideas.explanation: The top complaint about marriage is lack of sex. Searches for 'sexless marriage' are 3.5 times more common than 'unhappy marriage', and complaints about a spouse not wanting sex are 16 times more common than about one not wanting to talk. The top complaint about boyfriends is that they won't have sex. Only 25% of men and 8% of women admit to searching for porn, yet more men search for porn than for weather. Amit stresses that searches and fantasies are not what people want in real life.
core_ideas.quote: Searches for sexless marriage are three and a half times more common than unhappy marriage, and eight times more common than loveless marriage.

core_ideas.explanation: Parents are 2.5 times more likely to ask Google whether their son is gifted than their daughter. They ask whether their daughter is overweight about twice as often as their son. This contradicts the facts: young girls have larger vocabularies, are more often in gifted programmes, and about 28% of girls versus 25% of boys are overweight. Amit suspects the bias is worse in India.
core_ideas.quote: Parents are two and a half times more likely to ask, is my son gifted than is my daughter gifted?

core_ideas.concept: You can't be loved if you hide yourself
core_ideas.explanation: Many people never show their true selves to anyone, and some don't admit them even to themselves. Searching is the only place it shows. Amit draws the consequence: people can only love what you let them see.
core_ideas.quote: if you are not your authentic self, you can never be truly loved.

core_ideas.concept: Data shows you the median Indian
core_ideas.explanation: Everyone lives in a bubble, and society is too large to know firsthand. Aggregate data shows people unlike yourself. Ajay adds that it reflects the median Indian, who is very different from people like the hosts.
core_ideas.quote: Whereas this data reflects the median Indian and you know the median Indian is a very different person from us.

core_ideas.concept: From communities of circumstance to communities of choice
core_ideas.explanation: Before the internet, geography, school and work decided who you could meet, love or befriend. Dating apps remove that limit. You are unlikely ever to meet a single destined soulmate, but your chances of meeting someone good rise sharply. Women can date with more privacy and less judgement, and Amit cites a figure that 60% of recent marriages began online. The gain is biggest for LGBTQ people.
core_ideas.quote: If you are a gay person say born in 1960, you could spend your whole life alone. If you're a gay person born in the year 2000 You're not gonna spend your whole life alone.

core_ideas.explanation: Women swipe right on about 5 to 14% of profiles and men on about 50%, and men are 6.2 times more likely to like a woman than the reverse. A few men get most of the attention while the median man gets almost none, and nearly all women get picked. The resulting resentment fuels incels and the manosphere.
core_ideas.quote: There's a Tinder Gini coefficient of 0.58, which shows more inequality than 95% of the countries in the world.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay asks what has changed, since desire hasn't changed in 65,000 years. Amit's answer: a biologist would say men are wired to seek youth and beauty and women status and affluence, and he stresses that this is a description, not an endorsement. When your choices came from a small social circle, ordinary men found partners. With a million profiles, everyone is extremely selective and goes for people they could never have met before. Amit concludes the instincts haven't changed but the behaviour has. He also notes that culture can soften the uglier parts of human nature.
core_ideas.quote: I have much less scope to be selective. But I go to a dating app, I have a million people to choose from.

core_ideas.explanation: Men high on the 'dark triad' traits of psychopathy, narcissism and Machiavellianism may be 10 to 20% of dating-app users, and they are good at faking romantic qualities. Women they mistreat protect themselves by turning cold and exploiting ordinary men. Those men then treat ordinary women the same way to get even. The apps' anonymity and superficiality spread this until everyone is cold and calculating.
core_ideas.quote: Bad behavior drives out the good.

core_ideas.concept: Marriage as a bundle that is coming apart
core_ideas.explanation: Marriage arose when people met few others and social norms were enforced. It was an uneasy arrangement that left both sexes partly unsatisfied but held together. It combines love, sex, companionship, friendship and parenting. In modern society that arrangement may no longer work, and nobody has figured out how to organise relationships once those parts separate. Amit suspects today's dating apps may one day look primitive.
core_ideas.quote: marriage is a bundle of all of these things like love, sex, companionship, friendship, shared parenthood

core_ideas.explanation: Despite apps promising plenty of options, many people are dropping out. Gen Z has much less sex than millennials, and Amit says some are returning to family values. In one survey, three in ten men and one in four women said they hadn't had sex in a year. The Romantic Recession report describes falling trust: women avoid strangers and men feel shut out.
core_ideas.quote: People are having less and less sex than they used to.

core_ideas.concept: Measurement that changes what it measures
core_ideas.explanation: A satellite photographing North Korea at night doesn't change North Korea. Dating apps are different. They made romantic behaviour visible in data for the first time, and in doing so they changed that behaviour. When a tool makes something newly measurable, ask whether it is also reshaping it.
core_ideas.quote: So here the dating apps have simultaneously created observability, but then they have completely changed the system as well.

core_ideas.concept: The When Harry Met Sally index
core_ideas.explanation: Facebook mapped closeness across 1.4 trillion connections among 1.8 billion adults to build a cross-gender friendship index. Zero means men and women are completely segregated, and one means equal numbers of same-sex and opposite-sex friends. India scores 0.35, higher than Amit expected given how awkward Indian men are with women. Ajay calls the separation of the sexes in India a social crisis and wants researchers to use the district-level data.
core_ideas.quote: The purdah that we have in India that the two genders stand apart is something that is just completely broken. It interferes with the emergence of the good society.

core_ideas.concept: Apply the economist's toolkit to human nature
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's closing argument is that the right policies are already known and won't be implemented, so data-minded people are often working on the wrong problems. The deeper unsolved questions are about society and ourselves. He wants tools from psychology, sociology, anthropology, genetics, data, economics and literature applied to that question, citing Georges Simenon's theme that no one can fully communicate himself to another person.
core_ideas.quote: But I think the deeper questions we need to solve are questions about society. We don't understand ourselves. We don't understand other people.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay's opening dig: 'in this team the internal name for Amit Varma is the Energizer Bunny because he goes on and on.' Amit responds with a running gag about Ajay lasting only five seconds, which comes back all episode.
Amit, explaining the private self: 'very few people now know that you only last five seconds. Which was private until now. Now it's public.'
Amit's definition of Ajay's term 'digital exhaust': 'which is basically a phone running out of battery.'
After noting that more men search for porn than for weather, Amit tells Ajay he must search a lot for weather: 'But you can't jerk off to clouds. So there's an understandable reason for that.'

On the Australian autocomplete results 'an open marriage' and 'an open marriage novel': 'from this I can only gather that Australians want to read books about the things that they are bothered about.'

Amit's favourite finding from the book, which he says shows two deep truths about men, 'the self obsession and the stupidity': men search as often for how to perform oral sex on themselves as for how to give women an orgasm.
Stephens-Davidowitz on the long list of women's anxieties about how their bodies smell: 'we are all so busy judging our own bodies that there is little energy left over to judge other people.'
On parental regret: 'So full buyer's remorse happening if you can call parenting buying.'

Amit after reading the search data: 'the next time I'm in a bus, I will look around me and I will think, huh, twenty percent of these men want to be breastfed. What the fuck, dude? I'll be like judging every guy out there.'
Asked if he has used a dating app, Ajay says 'For about ten seconds.' Amit: 'So you lasted twice as long as one would expect. Well done. This used to be a family show till this episode.'
Amit on meeting Ajay online, 'though not on a dating app': 'Though I would always swipe right on you. But anyway, if swipe right is the correct direction.'

On the name 'WHMSI': 'I was calling it the Whimsy Index till I realized that the I at the end of it stands for index. So it would be like calling it When Harry Met Sally Index Index, which we don't want to do.'
After Ajay's Parade's End reading, Amit times it at about fifteen seconds and suggests Ajay add it to his 'act' to stretch the five-second gag.
Ajay defines the Gini coefficient on the spot, 'the area between the forty-five degree line and the cumulative distribution of income', before Amit applies it to Tinder.

Gabriel García Márquez's three selves (public, private, secret). Amit adds that the private self is known to a handful of intimates, 'Dunbar's smaller number, not one fifty, but five', and the secret self is known to nobody 'except Google Baba'.
'Dance like no one's looking': Amit's description of how we search online, as if nobody is watching.

Stephens-Davidowitz's line: 'Facebook is digital brag-to-my-friends-about-how-good-my-life-is serum,' where everyone seems happily married and on holiday in the Caribbean, while in reality people are ignoring calls from spouses they haven't slept with in years.

When Harry Met Sally, written by Nora Ephron, directed by Rob Reiner, starring Billy Crystal and Meg Ryan. Amit calls its restaurant scene 'the greatest orgasm in movie history', admits a crush on Meg Ryan, and quotes the premise that men and women can't be friends because 'the sex part always gets in the way.'

Ford Madox Ford's Parade's End, read by Ajay: 'You seduced a young woman in order to be able to finish your talks with her... You have to wait together for a week, for a year, for a lifetime, before the final intimate conversation may be attained and exhausted.'
Ajay invokes the Heisenberg uncertainty principle to contrast dating apps with satellite photos of North Korea at night: the apps change the behaviour they measure.
Rob Henderson, 'a guy who coined the term luxury beliefs', and his dark triad of psychopathy, narcissism and Machiavellianism applied to dating apps.
Georges Simenon, whom Amit calls one of his favourite novelists, on the theme running through all his work: 'it is impossible for any one person to communicate himself to another person.'
